premise: Everyone wants a hobby. Almost nobody gets past the enthusiastic first fortnight, because they mistake the feeling of starting for the work of continuing. This campaign takes one thing from curiosity to visible competence, and the method transfers to everything else.

reps.label: Practised
reps.hint: Any length. Fifteen honest minutes counts.

reps.label: Worked on the part I am bad at
reps.hint: Not the fun part. The weak part.

reps.label: Showed someone
reps.hint: Finished or not. Exposure is the accelerant.

reps.label: It went badly
reps.hint: Ruined, wrong, embarrassing. Log it — this is the curve.

reps.label: Finished something
reps.hint: Started things do not count. Finished ones do.

principles.title: Pick one and stop shopping
principles.body: Choosing is not the hard part, and researching which hobby to start is a way of not starting one. Pick the thing you have thought about more than twice, commit to thirty steps of it, and let the choice be arbitrary. Almost any craft teaches the same underlying lesson.

principles.title: Be bad on purpose, early
principles.body: The entry fee for every skill is a period of being visibly incompetent. Pay it fast and deliberately rather than avoiding it, because the avoidance is what keeps most people at zero for decades.

principles.title: Volume beats inspiration
principles.body: Do not wait to feel like it. The people who get good are the ones who booked the hours and turned up in a bad mood. Schedule the sessions the way you would a shift, and let motivation be a pleasant side effect rather than a requirement.

principles.title: Practise the part you are worst at
principles.body: Left alone, everyone practises what they can already do, because it feels good. Improvement lives entirely in the uncomfortable part. Fifteen minutes on your weakness is worth two hours on your strength.

principles.title: Finish things
principles.body: A finished mediocre thing teaches more than three abandoned brilliant ones. Finishing forces you through the unglamorous last twenty per cent, which is where the actual skill is, and it is the exact stretch that enthusiasm never covers.

principles.title: Get real feedback
principles.body: Praise from people who love you is emotionally useful and technically worthless. You need someone better than you to say specifically what is wrong. Ask for that directly, and do not defend yourself while they answer.

principles.title: Go public before you are ready
principles.body: Nobody feels ready. Publishing, performing or entering forces a standard that private practice never will, and the deadline does more for your ability than another month of comfortable rehearsal.

principles.title: Teach it
principles.body: Teaching is the audit. You cannot fake competence in front of a beginner asking why, and explaining something forces you to actually understand it rather than merely execute it.

missions.do: Pick the thing. Write it down. Stop considering alternatives.
missions.why: Researching hobbies is a way of not having one. Choose and close the tab.

missions.do: Spend twenty minutes doing it, badly, today.
missions.why: Before equipment, before research. Just make contact with the actual activity.

missions.do: Get the minimum kit. Not the good kit.
missions.why: Beginners overbuy to delay starting. Buy the cheap version and use it.

missions.do: Book three practice sessions into your calendar this week.
missions.why: Scheduled, like a shift. Motivation is not a plan.

missions.do: Do all three sessions, including the one you do not feel like.
missions.why: The one you do not feel like is the only one that proves anything.

missions.do: Find out how the good version is actually done.
missions.why: One hour of proper instruction beats ten hours of confidently wrong practice.

missions.do: Identify the specific thing you are worst at and name it.
missions.why: You cannot practise a weakness you have not defined.

missions.do: Spend an entire session only on that weakness.
missions.why: Uncomfortable, unrewarding, and the only place improvement actually happens.

missions.do: Show one person what you have made or learned so far.
missions.why: Early exposure, before it is good. It removes the fear from later showings.

missions.do: Finish one small thing completely.
missions.why: The last twenty per cent is where the skill lives. Go through it once.

missions.do: Practise four days this week.
missions.why: Density starts producing visible change. Push the frequency up.

missions.do: Find someone who is better and watch them work.
missions.why: You will see in ten minutes what you would not have noticed in ten months.

missions.do: Ask a practitioner to tell you what is wrong with your work.
missions.why: Ask, then be quiet. Do not explain what you were going for.

missions.do: Act on that feedback in your next three sessions.
missions.why: Feedback you do not implement was entertainment, not instruction.

missions.do: Practise on a day when everything is going badly.
missions.why: Skills built only in good conditions collapse in ordinary ones.

missions.do: Take a class or session with other people present.
missions.why: Being visibly a beginner in a room is its own separate skill.

missions.do: Measure something. Speed, accuracy, output — write the number down.
missions.why: Feeling like you improved is unreliable. A number is not.

missions.do: Finish something bigger than the first one.
missions.why: Scale up the finish. Same discipline, more of it.

missions.do: Do it on a day you would previously have called yourself too busy.
missions.why: Busy is a priority statement. Test whether it was true.

missions.do: Push one session until you genuinely cannot continue.
missions.why: Find the real edge of your capacity. It is further out than you assume.

missions.do: Show your work publicly, unfinished.
missions.why: Working in view removes the option of quietly abandoning it.

missions.do: Set a public deadline for something and tell someone the date.
missions.why: Announced deadlines behave completely differently from private ones.

missions.do: Meet the deadline. Whatever state it is in.
missions.why: Shipped and imperfect beats perfect and theoretical, every time.

missions.do: Enter, perform, submit or exhibit. Somewhere with an outcome.
missions.why: Strangers who did not choose to see it. This is the escalation.

missions.do: Do it again after it went badly.
missions.why: Everyone quits here. Returning is the entire difference between people.

missions.do: Make something for a specific person's actual need.
missions.why: Useful to someone else is the point where a hobby becomes a capability.

missions.do: Teach the first step to a complete beginner.
missions.why: You cannot fake this in front of someone asking why.

missions.do: Do the thing you called too advanced when you started.
missions.why: Go back and look at step one. It is within reach now.

missions.do: Count the sessions, the finishes and the failures. All of them.
missions.why: Thirty steps of evidence. This is what the work actually looked like.

missions.do: Commit to the next six months with a real target and a date.
missions.why: Thirty steps made you competent. Six months makes you someone who does this.
